title: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List
description: Brute force to optimized: a recursive depth-first value collection versus an in-place splicing technique that flattens the structure directly during a single forward walk.

sections.title: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List

content.title: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

You are given a doubly linked list, which, in addition to the next and previous pointers, could have a CHILD pointer, possibly pointing to a separate doubly linked list. Flatten the list so that all the nodes appear in a single-level doubly linked list. Flatten the list so that only the next and previous pointers are used (children are spliced in right after their parent node, and a child's own child list, if any, is flattened first).

blocks.caption: Whenever a node has a child, its entire child branch is spliced in directly after it, before continuing forward

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","The head of a multilevel doubly linked list (nodes may have a child pointer to a separate sub-list)"],["Output","The head of the resulting single-level doubly linked list"],["Goal","Flatten every child branch into the main list, in depth-first order, using O(1) extra space (excluding recursion, if used)"],["Constraints","The number of nodes will not exceed 1000; 1 <= Node.val <= 10^5"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A node can have a nested \"child\" list, itself possibly containing further nested child lists","A depth-first traversal: whenever a child is found, it (and everything nested within IT) must be fully processed before continuing to the current node's own next"],["The final structure must be a SINGLE flat list (just next/prev pointers)","Splicing: reconnect pointers directly, in place, rather than building a brand new list from scratch"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Whenever a node has a child pointer, that ENTIRE child branch (which may itself contain further nested children) must be inserted directly after that node, before whatever originally followed it, following a depth-first flattening order.

blocks.title: Analogy: Flattening a Nested Outline Into a Single To-Do List
blocks.text: Imagine a to-do list where some items have their own indented sub-list of steps underneath them, and those sub-steps might have their OWN further-indented sub-steps. "Flattening" this into one single linear list means: for each item, if it has sub-steps, insert them immediately after it (fully expanded, sub-steps of sub-steps included), before moving on to what was originally the NEXT item at the current level.

blocks.caption: Splicing a child branch in place: the parent connects to the child's head, and the child branch's tail reconnects to whatever originally followed the parent

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: main list 1-2-3-4-5-6, node 3 has child 7-8-9-10, node 8 (within that child branch) has its OWN child 11-12

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Node 3's child branch (7-8-9-10) is spliced in right after node 3","So far: 1,2,3,7,8,9,10,4,5,6","Depth-first: fully process node 3's child before continuing to node 3's original next (which was 4)"],["Within that branch, node 8's OWN child (11-12) is spliced in right after node 8","Final: 1,2,3,7,8,11,12,9,10,4,5,6","The nested child is processed before continuing to node 8's original next (node 9)"],["Answer","[1,2,3,7,8,11,12,9,10,4,5,6]","Every child branch fully expanded in depth-first order"]]}

blocks.text: Example: main list 1-2, node 1 has child 3 (no further nesting)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Node 1's child (just node 3) is spliced in right after node 1, before node 1's original next (node 2)","[1,3,2]","The child branch, however short, is fully inserted before continuing at the original level"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before building an entirely new list via a separate traversal-and-collect pass, notice that each child branch can be spliced directly into place, in a single forward walk, by carefully redirecting a few pointers at each node that has a child.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Walking forward through the list, the moment a node with a child is found, that child branch needs to be inserted RIGHT THERE, before whatever originally came next.

Observation 2: Splicing requires three pointer updates: the current node's next becomes the child's head; the child branch's TAIL (found by walking to the end of the child branch) needs its next set to whatever the current node's ORIGINAL next was; and that original next node's prev needs updating to point back to the child branch's tail.

Observation 3: After splicing, simply continuing the SAME forward walk (node = node.next) naturally walks INTO the just-spliced child branch next, which is exactly the depth-first order required, including correctly handling any further nested children within that branch.

Observation 4: No recursion or extra stack is strictly needed, since continuing the walk forward after splicing naturally reaches nested children in the correct order on its own.

Recognizing that "splice in place, then simply keep walking forward" naturally produces depth-first order (without needing an explicit stack) is the key simplifying insight.
This is an in-place splicing technique: whenever a child is found, its branch is spliced directly into the main list, and continuing the SAME forward walk naturally achieves depth-first flattening.
6. Brute Force Solution
Recursively walk the structure in depth-first order (whenever a child is found, fully recurse into it before continuing), collecting values into a new list as they are visited.
Step by step algorithm

items: Walk the current level: for each node, record its value.
If the node has a child, recursively process that ENTIRE child branch immediately (depth-first), before continuing to the current node's own next.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Recursing into a child BEFORE continuing to the current node's own next directly encodes the required depth-first flattening order.
Building a brand new result list (rather than modifying pointers) makes the recursive logic simpler to express, at the cost of not producing an actual re-linked doubly linked list.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly visits every node in the required depth-first order, since child branches are always fully recursed into before continuing at the current level.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), every node is visited exactly once.
Space: O(n) for the result list, plus O(d) recursion stack depth (d = maximum nesting depth).

Limitation: building a brand new result list does not actually produce the required re-linked doubly linked list structure (with correct next/prev pointers); an in-place splicing approach achieves the actual required structure directly.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force only collects values, not an actual re-linked structure. Instead, walk the list with a single pointer. Whenever the current node has a child, splice that child branch in directly: redirect the current node's next to the child's head, find the child branch's tail, and reconnect that tail to whatever originally followed the current node. Continuing the SAME forward walk then naturally proceeds into the newly spliced branch, achieving depth-first order without any explicit recursion or stack.

Walk node through the list. Whenever node.child exists: save next = node.next; set node.next = node.child and node.child.prev = node; clear node.child; walk to the child branch's tail; set tail.next = next (and next.prev = tail, if next exists). Then continue the outer walk with node = node.next as usual.
9. Optimized Solution
Splice each child branch in place as it is encountered, and simply continue walking forward to naturally achieve depth-first order.
Dry run for main list 1-2, node 1 has child 3

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action","State"],"rows":[["At node 1","node.child = node 3 exists; save next = node 2","-"],["Splice","node1.next = node3; node3.prev = node1; node1.child = null","1 -> 3 -> (still needs reconnecting)"],["Find child tail","Child branch is just node 3 itself (no further next)","tail = node 3"],["Reconnect","tail.next (node3.next) = saved next (node 2); node2.prev = node 3","1 -> 3 -> 2"],["Continue walk","node = node.next = node 3 (the just-spliced child); node 3 has no child, continue to node 2; node 2 has no child, done","-"]]}

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The flattened list is [1,3,2], matching the expected result.

codes.python:
def flatten(head):
    node = head
    while node:
        if node.child:
            next_node = node.next                                          # remember what originally came after this node
            child = node.child
            node.next = child                                              # splice: this node now connects directly to its child
            child.prev = node
            node.child = None

            tail = child                                                    # walk to the child branch's own tail
            while tail.next:
                tail = tail.next
            tail.next = next_node                                          # the child branch's tail reconnects to the ORIGINAL next
            if next_node:
                next_node.prev = tail
        node = node.next                                                    # continue forward (now walking INTO the just-spliced child)
    return head


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n3 = ListNode(3)
    n2 = ListNode(2)
    n1 = ListNode(1)
    n1.next = n2
    n2.prev = n1
    n1.child = n3
    result = flatten(n1)
    values = []
    node = result
    while node:
        values.append(node.val)
        node = node.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) overall: although finding each child branch's tail looks like it could add extra cost, each node's "next" pointer is followed at most a constant number of extra times in total, keeping the total work linear.
Space: O(1) extra, entirely in-place pointer manipulation (no recursion needed).
Why This Works

Continuing the SAME outer forward walk after a splice is the key trick: since the current node now points directly at the (just-spliced) child's head, the very next iteration naturally walks INTO that child branch. If a node within that branch ALSO has its own child, the exact same splicing logic applies again, naturally handling arbitrarily deep nesting without any explicit recursion or stack, purely by continuing the same simple forward walk.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A node has no child","Simply continue forward, no splicing needed"],["A node has a child","Splice the child branch in directly (3 pointer updates), then continue forward, walking into the branch next"],["A nested node ALSO has a child","The same splicing logic applies again naturally, since the outer walk is now positioned inside that nested branch"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Saving "next" (the node's ORIGINAL next) before modifying node.next is essential, since it would otherwise be lost the moment node.next is reassigned.
Finding the child branch's tail requires an inner walk (following .next until reaching a node with no next), which is where the child branch's reconnection point is.
Clearing node.child after splicing prevents ever re-processing the same child link again, keeping the structure a clean single-level doubly linked list.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (recursive depth-first collection)","O(n)","O(n) result + O(d) recursion","Collects values correctly, but does not produce an actual re-linked structure"],["Optimized (in-place splicing, single walk)","O(n)","O(1) extra","Directly produces the required re-linked doubly linked list, no recursion needed"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Flattening a nested (multilevel) linked structure can often be done in a SINGLE forward walk with no explicit recursion: splicing each child branch in place, then simply continuing the same walk, naturally achieves depth-first order because the walk flows directly into the newly spliced nodes.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to save the node's ORIGINAL next pointer before overwriting it during the splice, losing track of where the child branch's tail needs to reconnect.
Forgetting to update the reconnected node's prev pointer (not just its next), leaving the doubly linked list's backward pointers inconsistent.
Using unnecessary recursion when a simple continued forward walk already handles nested children correctly on its own.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Empty list","Returned as null/None directly, nothing to flatten"],["No node has any child at all","The list is already flat; the walk simply passes through without ever splicing"],["A child branch itself has no next (a single-node child)","Its tail is itself; reconnection still works correctly since the inner tail-finding walk handles this directly"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly stating that "continuing the outer walk after a splice naturally achieves depth-first order, without needing recursion" demonstrates a deeper understanding than simply describing a recursive solution.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Flatten a NESTED/multilevel linked structure" points toward in-place splicing during a single forward walk, letting the walk naturally flow into (and out of) each spliced child branch.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does continuing the same outer walk after splicing correctly handle arbitrarily deep nesting? Because the walk's very next step lands on the child's head, and if THAT node also has a child, the same splicing logic simply triggers again.

What is the actual total time complexity, given the extra "find the child branch's tail" inner walk? Still O(n) overall, since every node's next pointer is followed a bounded number of times in total across the whole process (each node is either the outer walk's current position exactly once, or part of exactly one tail-finding inner walk).

How would you adapt this if children could ALSO have a "sibling child" (multiple child branches per node)? A different data model would be needed, and a stack-based or explicit recursive approach would likely become necessary to track multiple pending branches.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A specialized in-place splicing technique, conceptually related to the general linked-list re-linking skills built throughout this category, applied here to a genuinely nested (tree-like) linked structure rather than a flat one.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space + O(d) recursion.
Optimized (in-place splicing, single walk): O(n) time, O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: In-place splicing during a single forward walk

Core Idea: Whenever a child is found, splice its branch directly into the main list (redirect next/prev pointers around it), then simply continue the SAME walk, which naturally flows into the branch and achieves depth-first order without recursion
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Continuing the outer walk after a splice automatically produces depth-first traversal order, since the walk's next step lands directly on the spliced-in child
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: On a child: next=node.next; node.next=child; find child's tail; tail.next=next; continue walking
